i'm not a fan of vinyl.

(first my bona fides- i am old enough to 'member berries before cd's existed. i actually worked in an honest to goodness record store in the mid-80's, the last year i worked there was just when cds became popular enough to not be considered niche audiophile products. i still have a fantastic turntable- a technics sl-1700 mk 2 direct drive- which i've owned for 30 years and a large collection of vinyl records.)

the second you take a record out of it's sleeve it's fidelity starts to degrade and using a physical process to read it- diamond needles to be specific- only exacerbates this wear. additionally, dust. not to mention that cleaning a record every time you play it is a pain in the ass and also adds wear to it. having to flip a record after approximately 25 minutes is also a pain in the ass.

finally the quality of the vinyl used to make most records is terrible. you may not know this but if you have a high quality vinyl record you should be able to hold it up to a light source and see through it. it should appear uniformly translucent with no foggy areas. if it isn't see though or has dark patches it's not a high quality product. when records were the only game in town most high quality vinyl releases were expensive special half speed remastered versions of popular records, a few jazz labels, and some classical music labels (i'm looking at you deutche grammophon.) popular albums were almost never printed on high quality vinyl.

back in the day the modus operandi was to buy a new record and at the same time buy a high quality liner (because paper liners added to record wear) and a cassette. the first time you played the record at home you taped it at the same time and then almost always used the cassette to listen to the record so it would last longer without developing pops and clicks from wear. records were treated essentially as master recordings from which you would make copies to actually listen to.

finally the sound is not better. if you listed to a compact disc vs. even a high quality vinyl record there are things you will hear- or not hear in the case of quiet sections- on the cd that you can not hear on the vinyl record. vinyl records just can not physically produce the frequency response that a cd can.

do vinyl records sound better than cds?

The Technics SL-1700 mk 2 is a mediocre turntable at best so isn't a good turntable to test versus CD. Also, unless you remove the mould release agent from the pressings you've never actually played the vinyl. You need a solvent to get that crap off because it collects dust and hardens filling in the fine details and making the LP sound dull over time. Remove it and you'll expose the pristine vinyl surface even on old crackly records. You do need a good turntable and cartridge to really get the best out of an LP and most people don't. You're right that most vinyl LPs, particularly those pressed in the 1980's were terrible. They packed more tracks on to compete with the playing time of CD so made the grooves closer together and shallower which lead to higher surface noise levels and crushed dynamics. Hunt out some of the Mobile Fidelity Sound Labs pressings though which are half speed mastered on virgin vinyl from the original master tapes and you'll be amazed how they sound. If you want to get beat the quality of those pressings you're really needing to use DSD which is how CD should have sounded. Unfortunately, the old 16 bit red book CD-A was good enough to sound better than an average turntable of the time but not as good as a high end deck. DSD though (as found on SACDs and more recently just plain downloads) is another matter entirely and sounds fabulous. Unfortunately, they're rare since most people are happy with the sound of CD or even MP3 but there are a number of albums you can download in DSD format. My Oppo plays DSD natively and it is very clearly better than CD and LP.
